title: J Jumbled Block Hierarchy
statementMd:
Jumbled Block Hierarchy
       Input ﬁle:           standard input
       Output ﬁle:          standard output

Consider all permutations P1 , P2 , . . . , Pn of the integers from 1 to n.

You are given m inclusive intervals of positions, called blocks. The blocks are laminar: any two blocks are
either identical, have no position in common, or one is entirely contained in the other. In particular, two
blocks never partially overlap.

A permutation respects the blocks if, for every given block [l, r], the set

                                                {Pl , Pl+1 , . . . , Pr }

is a set of consecutive integers. The order of these values inside the block is unrestricted. Equivalently,
the block must satisfy
                                             max Pi − min Pi = r − l.
                                           l≤i≤r        l≤i≤r
Only the blocks given in the input impose restrictions. Repeated copies of the same block do not add any
restriction.

An index i with 1 ≤ i < n is a descent of P if Pi > Pi+1 . For every d from 0 to n − 1, let Cd be the
number of permutations that respect all the given blocks and have exactly d descents.

No permutation is given in the input. Determine C0 , C1 , . . . , Cn−1 by counting all permutations that
satisfy the restrictions.

Input
The ﬁrst line contains two integers n and m (1 ≤ n ≤ 2 · 105 , 0 ≤ m ≤ 106 ), the length of the permutation
and the number of blocks.

Each of the next m lines contains two integers li and ri (1 ≤ li ≤ ri ≤ n), describing the inclusive interval
of positions of block i.

The blocks are given in an arbitrary order. It is guaranteed that they form a laminar family. Duplicate
blocks may appear.

Output
Print one line containing n integers C0 , C1 , . . . , Cn−1 in this order, each taken modulo 998 244 353.

Examples
                    standard input                                          standard output
 5 3                                                   1 6 10 6 1
 1 5
 1 4
 1 3
 3 0                                                   1 4 1


                                                      Page 1 of 2
 Note
In the ﬁrst example, there are 24 permutations that respect all three blocks. The numbers having exactly
0, 1, 2, 3, 4 descents are respectively
                                              1, 6, 10, 6, 1.

In the second example, there are no blocks, so every permutation of 1, 2, 3 is allowed. Among the six
permutations, one has no descents, four have one descent, and one has two descents.
